segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Chana Joffe-Walt sitting in for Ira Glass. Ira is here, but I'm taking over today's show because we're talking about questions that I think are pretty fundamental to all of us at various points in our lives but are especially pressing for me these days. I'd like to explain with a brief example of a situation I find myself in all the time lately, with my two children, feeling deeply lost.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's bath time. Jacob, the older one, is running a restaurant. He's giving out great prizes-- cups for grownups, and also animals.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Animals.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I want to hug an animal.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Jacob says, if someone in your family is Christian, you can get one of those.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: But if somebody in your family is Christian, you're going to give those to them.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Is your family Christian?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Is your mom or your dad Christian?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Is your brother or your sister Christian?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: No. They're all Jewish.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: He snatches the animal and says, sorry.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Wait. I can't have any animals unless I'm Christian?

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: You can't have that duck, sorry.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why can't I have the duck?

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Because you're not Christian.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: No Jews allowed, says my 3 and 1/2-year-old to my Jewish face. So here is my question-- what am I supposed to say right here? Because I should say something, right? I should say, that is not OK, because-- why?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Because I said so? Because you're a Jew? Because Jews like your great grandparents were driven from their communities by exactly the mentality you've just expressed to me, my 3 and 1/2-year-old boy? Or because we live in a majority Christian country, and I'm worried that I've clearly already failed to provide you with a positive relationship to Judaism?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Or is the best approach not to say anything? He's just having a bath. I don't know, as you will hear.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But sweetie, it's not nice to say that somebody can't have something because they're not Christian.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Well, you can't have the animals because you're not Christian.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That makes me feel sad, though, sweetie.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Well, many people who are Christian can have those animals. In this restaurant, that's what the rules are.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That's not kind, though.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Yeah, but that's what the rules are at this restaurant.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Well, there's so many rules in this anti-Semitic restaurant.

segments.speaker: Jacob
segments.text: Sorry. They're kind for some people.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: He says, they're kind for some people, just not my kind of people. The problem with talking to kids about anything that's actually important is that they don't know anything. It's your job to teach them about all of the stuff that matters most, but you have nothing to work with.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They don't know religion. They don't know history. They don't know how to maintain proper hygiene.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Also a problem, they're little, and they have feelings. So you have to be careful about saying, well, let me tell you a story about a man named Adolf Hitler. He would have liked the way you run your restaurant, by the way.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: We've all been on the kid side of this kind of conversation, where a grownup is fumbling through something that is clearly important. The big one most of us remember is when someone told us about sex. And on the adult side, whatever the question is-- what is sex, what is God, or what is ISIS, what does transgendered mean-- you know in that moment that what you say could really matter, could be the thing this person remembers and carries with them into adulthood, could shape the way they feel about their safety or their sexuality. These conversations are how we make our mark on the next generation. They're also, very often, how we learn how much we do not know.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And in today's show, we're going to listen in as people take on three of the most difficult things to talk about. We're going to hear teenagers talking very frankly to each other about sex, parents talking to their children about race, and kids talking to each other about death. Today's show, "The Birds and the Bees." We've got Jonathan Goldstein, comedian W. Kamau Bell. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Act One, "Some Like It Not, On the Neck." To begin, I should say, throughout this hour we're going to be talking about subject matter that can be difficult to discuss with children. So if you've got kids listening, that's something to consider. Also in this next story, as Ira says, we will be acknowledging the existence of sex and talking a lot about our reluctance to speak of its existence.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK, let's start with the beginning. One way a lot of kids learn about the birds and bees is from each other. A couple weeks ago, a seven-year-old named Moxie told me a friend of hers, this kid, Aaron, said something to her that bothered her on the bus. He said, if he drew a picture of a baby on a piece of paper and put it in her belly, that would make a baby.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Moxie knew this was incorrect. That's why it bothered her. So a week later at the playground across the street from her house, she sat Aaron down.

segments.speaker: Moxie
segments.text: The situation about the paper not working thing.

segments.speaker: Aaron
segments.text: What's that means?

segments.speaker: Moxie
segments.text: On the bus a few days ago, you talked about paper and body and about a baby.

segments.speaker: Aaron
segments.text: Oh, right, right, right.

segments.speaker: Moxie
segments.text: That was a silly plan.

segments.speaker: Aaron
segments.text: I'm sure it's going to work, but I don't know.

segments.speaker: Moxie
segments.text: Uh, I'm not sure, because the baby can't survive, you see? I'm just saying.

segments.speaker: Aaron
segments.text: Sorry.

segments.speaker: Moxie
segments.text: You need to make a sperm. And the sperm somehow has to get into my body. And that's how it works.

segments.speaker: Aaron
segments.text: I did not know that.

segments.speaker: Moxie
segments.text: Well, now you do.

segments.speaker: Aaron
segments.text: Sorry.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When it comes to sex, a lot of us learn the wrong thing first and the right thing later. You learn through a series of corrections. You start to find out that half the things your brother told you were not right, that that scene in the movie is not realistic, that [? Sophia De Santos ?] was lying when she said she did that thing, because that thing is not possible.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That's basically our system. You learn things wrong, test them out, and hopefully get the real story from someone named Moxie. This begins on the playground and just continues all the way until you actually start having sex, and all the weird information that was not corrected begins to matter.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What are you hoping they're going to cover?

segments.speaker: Deondre
segments.text: I hope they cover everything.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Deondre is in a classroom at Buffalo State with about 50 other people, mostly men, mostly his fraternity brothers. He's here for some sex ed.

segments.speaker: Deondre
segments.text: I feel like some stuff people don't know.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What don't you know?

segments.speaker: Deondre
segments.text: I don't know. That's a good question, you know.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This is a voluntary workshop about sexual assault and consent, on a Monday night. You'd think this event might not win out over, say, hitting up the Jamba Juice or staring at your van Gogh poster.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But this room is packed. The students are wide awake. Knees are bouncing. Hands are shooting up in the air. The instructor, Paula Madrigal, is talking about the importance of consent.

segments.speaker: Paula Madrigal
segments.text: So consent is a verbal and enthusiastic yes, OK? Why is it enthusiastic?

segments.speaker: Student 1
segments.text: Because you actually want to do it.

segments.speaker: Paula Madrigal
segments.text: Exactly. You want to do it. And sex should be fun, right?

segments.speaker: Student 2
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Paula Madrigal
segments.text: Yeah. I hope so.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This kind of workshop was repeated in classrooms all across campus here and throughout the country in the last year. College administrators are panicked about sexual assault, as they should be. So they're turning to this kind of education as the answer instead of mostly focusing on protecting women, things like rape whistles or travel with a buddy programs.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They also want to teach men actual sentences to say. Do you like this? Can I kiss you? But the students here are struggling with the basic premise.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They have to learn to speak in this new way because if you don't you're a rapist? Because it's just more virtuous? They have questions right from the start.

segments.speaker: Paula Madrigal
segments.text: It's a continuous process of checking up, or checking in, either/or. What does that mean?

segments.speaker: Student 2
segments.text: You keep asking her? That's weird.

segments.speaker: Student 3
segments.text: That kind of messes up the mood. I'm not trying to be funny, but if she says yes, and you know, she keeps saying, yeah, I've got to be like, hey, you sure? Are you really sure? We're about to do this.

segments.speaker: Student 4
segments.text: Every 10 minutes.

segments.speaker: Student 3
segments.text: I'm almost there. I'm about to go to the drawer to get the protection. No, no. You're right. You're right. You're right.

segments.speaker: Student 2
segments.text: And you're like, no.

segments.speaker: Student 3
segments.text: No. Obviously, I'm going to stop. But the re-affirmation of yes over and over again, that kind of would mess up the mood. So I feel like should there be a number of times that you should-- you know?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: He presses them on this. Two? Three? Seven? But that guy is overtaken by his fraternity brothers, who also have urgent questions. Does body language count as consent?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What if she said yes before you got into the room when you were both sober, like in a message on Twitter or something? How many beers is too much to have consent? Again, please offer a number.

segments.speaker: Student 5
segments.text: Like, you ever heard the term alcohol is liquid courage? Like, what if it's in the sense where it's like you were probably nervous, and you don't want to be nervous around her. So that's your liquid courage. All right, I'm not going to be shaky when she come over. You feel me? So you're not using it to get a yes.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The next guy over interrupts. What if both parties are drunk? And then across the room-- does the girl need to ask for consent? Another student-- OK, what if we've been together for a year?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Paula Madrigal replies, you always need consent, even if you're a woman, even if you're a man sleeping with men, even if you're in a relationship, even if you have sex every day, even if you are in the middle sex.

segments.speaker: Paula Madrigal
segments.text: Or if you guys are engaging in sexual activity, and maybe all of a sudden someone decides I want to try it rough, if you guys already started having sex, the other person can withdraw that consent. OK? So that's why it's active.

segments.speaker: Paula Madrigal
segments.text: What if someone's like, I want to have another person here, now let's have three people? You're already having sex. So if all of a sudden they're like, surprise, I have another person, you can be like, yeah, um, I didn't really sign up for that. I'm out of here. OK? Does that make a little bit more sense when we talk about, you know, checking in and the active process?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Those are carefully chosen examples. The vast majority of sexual assault on college campuses occur between two people who know each other. And there's not always physical force.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So Paula is trying to say, take the picture you have in your mind of a serial predator rapist. Put it to the side for a moment. Imagine instead a person who wakes up in the morning and wonders quietly to himself, she was into that, right? Yeah, she was into that. Imagine that person is wrong.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The workshop was supposed to be 45 minutes. It's been an hour. Paula Madrigal is trying to wrap up.

segments.speaker: Paula Madrigal
segments.text: So how do you guys, then-- you guys are the experts. How do you ask for consent?

segments.speaker: Student 6
segments.text: It doesn't sound right. It's like you're messing up the whole mood when you ask that.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's been an hour, and the students in this room are still fixated on this question of the mood. I don't remember there being a whole lot of mood when it came to sex in college. I don't know, maybe you guys all had candle-lit dorm rooms.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But there is genuine panic behind that question. It's dismissed in a workshop about sexual assault, because of course it is. We're taking about assault. You're talking about the mood. Those are two separate conversations.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But these guys are trying to have just one conversation about everything, a conversation that takes into account consent, but also all of their questions and anxieties when it comes to talking to a person they're sleeping with. It seems like that's a conversation they've never had.

segments.speaker: Nagib Gonzalez
segments.text: That is one of the hardest things ever, is to try to find out-- how would you say find out what the other person wants?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This is the Nagib Gonzalez, a college freshman in Buffalo. I known Nagib from previous reporting. He's lovely. And like every freshman at his school, he's been to a consent training in the last year.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I feel like if we're going to lay the burden of changing the way we talk about sex at the feet of 18-year-olds, people who are already many years into learning weird and bad and confusing information, if that's our answer to reduce sexual assault, I wanted to know more about what these guys actually know and where they learned it.

segments.speaker: Nagib Gonzalez
segments.text: Men talk about women all the time. I just thought, like, my roommate always talks to me about his favorite sex position. And then my other friends would tell me their favorite sex positions, and then we'll just talk about, oh, that's cool. Oh, I'll try that one one day.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But that's men who are sleeping with women talking about what women like to other men.

segments.speaker: Nagib Gonzalez
segments.text: Yeah. So it's more like we'll decide what women do or don't like.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But when do you talk to women about what they like?

segments.speaker: Nagib Gonzalez
segments.text: Hmm. Yeah, OK, it's definitely men talk to men about what women like. I feel like that's how it is. Even if you get told by a woman what she likes, you'll be like, oh, I knew that.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Lately Nagib's biggest source of information is his roommate, Elijah Leslie. He brought Elijah up a lot. Elijah says he first learned about the birds and bees from his cousin.

segments.speaker: Elijah Leslie
segments.text: Then you get older. Then you see Sports Illustrated . Then you see the Playboy s. Then you see the porn. And then you see the Girls Gone Wild . Then you see those late night-- the Girls Gone Wild, the late night commercials and stuff like that. Like 4:00 in the morning, Girls Gone Wild. I think that's when you start learning.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Elijah was not the first or the last person I interviewed who told me he learned about sex from porn. So Nagib is learning how to engage with women from other men who are learning from porn. That's like learning Chinese from a white American in Wyoming. You're missing some key primary source information.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Every person I talk to who works on sexual assault prevention brought up one thing as particularly troubling about the way men learn about sex, and it wasn't porn. It was baseball, that we talk about sex like it's baseball, getting a home run as a metaphor for sex. They said, think of how many bad lessons are built into that metaphor. You go first base, second base, third base. There's only one direction to move. And a home run is a win.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Not to mention, you're on opposing teams. It's competitive. And it's a sport that mostly only men play.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Nagib Gonzalez is not attached to sex being like baseball or porn. Nagib just wants to be a good person. He wants to be good to people. He's looking for some guidance. Nagib is always looking for guidance. He solicits advice often.

segments.speaker: Nagib Gonzalez
segments.text: This is an example. I remember my cousin telling me, yo, you've got to kiss your girl's neck. I do it all the time. Oh, my girl loves it, and stuff like that. So then that's kind of where you learn.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Nagib, ever the careful student, kissed necks, every one of them. Another friend told him, women like it when you're funny. He tries to be that.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But then, Nagib had a girlfriend who told everybody he was a bad kisser. And someone told him, please stop kissing my neck. She thought it was gross. And he felt like, wait, do I know things? Or do I not know things?

segments.speaker: Nagib Gonzalez
segments.text: Definitely when you're younger, you think of it more as rules and steps to get laid. When you're younger, you think, oh, I have to do this step. I have to follow these steps. So I have to kiss her in this certain place. Then I have to make out with her.

segments.speaker: Nagib Gonzalez
segments.text: Then I have to-- I don't know-- touch her. I don't know. I don't know, grab her butt or something. And then, finally we get here.

segments.speaker: Nagib Gonzalez
segments.text: But it's not like that at all. It's less-- it's very-- I don't know. It varies. It's different from person to person. It could be anything. I don't know. Girls vary. Not every girl will like something that you do. Every girl is different.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Everyone is different. Girls vary. People vary. What if that was the first thing you learned about sex?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What if instead of starting at 18 years old with rape and moving backwards to teach consent, what if you just started with people vary? Because if you understand that, consent follows. You have to ask questions and talk about what you like and don't like. Otherwise, you'll never know. You may be with one of those neck people, and you may not.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: For the rest of today's show, we are going to leave sex behind, and we are going to step forward from the beginning of life to the murky, complicated middle, the other facts of life that you really don't want to have to explain to children, because you wish they were not facts or a part of life at all. Our next story is from W. Kamau Bell. He's a comedian and a father.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And recently, Kamau's been planning for a conversation he really does not want to have with his children, one that is familiar to black parents everywhere in America. Act Two, "If You See Racism, Say Racism." Here's Kamau.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: I talk about race and racism in my act a lot, some would say too much. It was how I was raised. Some families have hardware stores. My family has thinking about racism. So it's no surprise to me that after I became a parent, I began to do jokes about race and racism and fatherhood.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: "And people ask me all the time, like, you're black. You talk about race a lot. And have you talked to your daughter about the fact that she's black? I'm like, no, because she's 3 and 1/2. I don't want to bum her out yet. You know what I'm saying?

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: Being black is great, but it's like a big responsibility to know that. My mom waited until I was eight before she told me I was black. And she did it the right way.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: One night she's like, tonight for dinner, you can have whatever you want. I was like, yay. And she's like, you can stay up all night and watch TV. I was like, yay. And you're black. I was like, hold on a second. That explains everything.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: I thought every day I was just kind of having a shitty day. It's good to know why now. It's good to know there's a historical context for that."

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I now have two girls, a baby named Juno and an almost four-year-old named Sami. My wife, Melissa, is white. And Sami calls herself peanut butter. She really doesn't say much of anything yet.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: My wife and I have both put our toes, or at least our older daughter, Sami's, toe in the race pool. But we have not even put the slightest hint of a Sami toe into the racism pool. Yes, those are separate pools.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The race pool is filled with positive stories of black achievement, African American role models, books and TV shows featuring diverse characters. Our race pool even has Kwanzaa.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But Sami's racism pool is completely drained with a lock on the gate. And we run past it every day on the way to the race pool. And every day that goes by, I feel guilty. The racism pool is treacherous. It's not fun to swim in.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And if you aren't careful, you drown in the sorrow of the black experience in America. Damn. We live in Berkeley. People have been protesting the police blocks from our house. How do I explain that?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This was on my mind recently, how to teach Sami about racism, when this thing happened. It was January 26 of this year, my birthday. I was having a low key celebration, just like I like them.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I was carrying a children's book I had just bought for Sami, The Case for Loving: The Fight for Interracial Marriage. Mildred and Richard Loving are the interracial couple responsible for the Supreme Court striking down the laws in 16 states that banned interracial marriage. And if I was going to get into racism with Sami, then the Loving story-- which was about a family like ours-- seemed like a great place to start.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: So I'm sure that many of you have heard the story of the incident that happened on January 26.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: On a Friday in March, Melissa and I sat on a stage at a middle school in a packed auditorium. My main concern was that somehow all the planning and structure was going to lead to an event that was careful, sanitized, and maybe the worst thing, boring. It wasn't, due in large part to two amazing women on the panel, Kadijah Means-- who we'll get to in a minute-- but first, Nikki Jones.

segments.speaker: Nikki Jones
segments.text: OK. I'll put on my professor voice.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: Nikki Jones teaches at UC Berkeley. She said something that, for me, made sense of the world, not just about the small racial injustices that happen in cafes but the bigger, deadly ones that are happening all around America. She asked us to think of the world in terms of black space and white space.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: She credits Elijah Anderson for this theory, but tonight she made it her main point. Nikki says people have ideas about black spaces. It's tied to blackness and poverty and the ghetto. It's impossible to say the word ghetto in America without thinking about black people.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: See a black man in a suit, your brain does a calculus. What poor neighborhood did he or his parents rise up out of, or his parents' parents? It all goes back to the ghetto.

segments.speaker: Nikki Jones
segments.text: And the ghetto itself is believed to be carried on the bodies, on and in black people. And that presents special dilemmas when black people are in white space. And what's white space? Well, just about everywhere else. Right?

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: She says UC Berkeley, where she teaches, white space. Almost all education, public and private, white space. Movie theaters, restaurants, some of my own stand-up shows-- I'm looking at you, Spokane-- white space. Public Radio, white space. And of course, the Elmwood cafe.

segments.speaker: Nikki Jones
segments.text: So in these white spaces, black people have a special burden, and they face a number of dilemmas. They have to prove that they belong there. The burden is on them to prove that they belong in a particular space.

segments.speaker: Nikki Jones
segments.text: Now let's go back to the incident. Who belongs in that space? What is the presumption about what Kamau is carrying on his body?

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: Of course, not belonging can work both ways. A white person in a black space lacks a similar trustworthiness. But think of how rare it is that a white person goes to a black space. Like a tourist in another country, you can leave whenever you choose.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: But the highlight of the night, high school senior, Kadijah Means. She's 18 and made a name for herself in the Bay Area as an activist. She's an awesome public speaker who, importantly to me, knows how to open with a joke.

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: So number one, I want to say that I've been black all of my life. That's a pretty good amount of motivation for me to be a social justice advocate.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: And then she said something that made me take extra notice. She talked about being younger than my daughter, Sami, when she learned about race.

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: I learned about race at a really young age, maybe like two or three. My dad has a really good way of teaching about fractions. When he would make me toast, he would cut it in half and be like, this is half. This is a fourth.

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: So I learned about race in a kind of similar way, learning that white didn't mean white like paper, but it was a construct. Yeah, I learned that pretty young. That was weird.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: My oldest daughter is four. She has just begun to understand that people are different colors. I can't imagine somehow connecting that to the fact that race itself is a construct.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: I'm not sure I could define the word construct to another adult, let alone a four-year-old. Kadijah then closed with a few tips on how we can all be less racist, like this one.

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: Focus less on color blindness, because honestly, you're not going to get a gold star for that. Be more color competent. Be more--

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: Thanks.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: And this one.

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: Please don't call people articulate. Don't come up to me after and tell me I'm articulate. Please do not do that. And there's a whole bunch of reasons why that we don't have time for.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: You might want to grab a pen and some paper, because she's on a roll.

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: Your mind makes generalizations. That's what it does. It's not bad to that. It's bad to think that that one generalization is what everyone is.

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: You also have to take a step outside of that and remember that people are individuals. People have different lives. Just because I'm black doesn't mean I act like other black people. Black people built this country, whether you like it or not. Love us, please. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: I was so impressed by Kadijah. I began to think about her dad, the one who taught her about fractions and race. Kadijah was completely versed in the evils of racism. But she was also idealistic about the future.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: She understood how well-intended people could do racist things, but how that doesn't always make them bad people. She got the broad strokes and the nuances. And Kadijah also knew how to do something that is absolutely essential to your survival as a black person in America.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: She saw and identified racism in her everyday life, and she didn't internalize it. But she also didn't ignore it. She just judo flipped it and kept walking. I wanted some advice on how to raise a kid like that. Who was this dad? I imagined him to be a mix of '60s era Berkeley hippie and hope and change era Obama.

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: I don't smile a lot. So I'm not the smiling black man.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: Yeah. That's Cliff Means. He's a self-described businessman who means business.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: I like to imagine that his business card reads on one line, "Cliff Means," and under that, "Business." In fact, when we ask Cliff to do the interview, initially he said, "I don't know you. I don't know your audience. So no."

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: So when my producer, Robyn, and I met with Cliff and Kadijah, I knew he was still reluctant, but I wasn't sure what had changed his mind. I had to ask.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: Why are you doing this interview, then?

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: Kadijah really wanted me to do this is the bottom line. Now, had I found out anything too horrific about either one of you, then it probably still would have been no. But I couldn't find anything terrible.

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: Well, I tell you, one thing that leaned in your favor. I did read something written by you, because I was trying to do as much homework as I could, because my answer was really no. And your writing had made enough white people angry that I said, OK, maybe he's actually trying to do something.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: So it's clear that Cliff is not exactly a "why can't we just get along" type of guy. And he has very clear thoughts about what should be taught to kids.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: How old was Kadijah when you first started explaining race to her?

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: I would imagine four or five years old. She was an early talker. We spent a ton of time together, because I asked her, does she want to enter a speech for the Martin Luther King celebration at her school. And we co-wrote a speech that people were very enamored with.

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: And I explained to her that Martin Luther King wasn't killed for the "I Have a Dream" speech, but once he started talking about getting poor whites and poor blacks together, then he had to go. But my children, I taught, you will be going to school, and you will be getting told that there's justice for all. And then when you find out there's not, then you'll be confused. And I don't want my children confused. I want them knowledgeable.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: So at what age did you get into the history of black people in this country and have to cover things like pre-Civil Rights Movement, like Jim Crow and slavery and things like that?

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: At five, I taught her about slavery, and I taught her as what it is, that Europe went to war with West Africa for centuries. Kids used to love Native Americans when I was a kid because they fought back. Why didn't black people fight back?

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: Well, they did, and were slaughtered and terrorized and tortured and murdered and raped-- I probably left out rape at that age for her-- captured, kidnapped, and brought over Africans to America. And they were here terrorized and murdered. And we go from that stage all the way to being here, enslaved.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: He taught her that at five. Cliff is clearly not afraid to throw his kids into the deep end of the racism pool and let them learn to swim. This is pretty much the opposite of what I had done so far. How deep did their racism pool get?

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: She learned things like white officers following the black migration to northern California to work in the shipping yards, in southern California was shipping yards. Hey, we'd better bring some racist white cops here to keep these people in line.

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: She learned that there were black cooks grinding up glass in the kitchen to make sure that white racist, brutal slave masters' intestines would bleed and be open, and then he would be gone. What was your question?

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: Do you want the church thing brought up at all?

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: It's fine.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: That's Kadijah. I don't know what the church thing is, but I can tell it was one of those family stories. Kadijah let my producer, Robyn, and I in on it.

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: After my dad told me about racism, I distinctly remember being angry with white people, like how dare you enslave my people. And so we were at church one day.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: It wasn't actually at church. It was a church function. It was in the church. It was a church function held after.

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: So I guess I went up onto the pulpit and asked for the mic. And I told the entire congregation that black people and white people should not be together. And that was my synthesis of racism in America and slavery that I had come up with throughout the week after my dad told me about racism.

segments.speaker: Robyn
segments.text: You're saying you became a five-year-old segregationist?

segments.speaker: Kadijah Means
segments.text: I did. I did.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: In my house, we can't have a five-year-old segregationist. I mean, don't get me wrong, it'd be fun for a bit in a Kids Say the Darndest Things kind of way. I ran a version of what Kadijah said in church by my wife, Melissa, as a hypothetical.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: What would you do if Sami told you white people and black people can't be together? It would be an immediate investigation. Melissa would ask, "What makes you say that? Why do you think they can't be together? And yes, OK, white people did hurt your people. But also, Mommy and Daddy are together. And that's good, isn't it?"

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: It would be a conversation with me. It would be a conversation with Sami, every day, all the time. I asked Cliff how he felt about Kadijah's speech at church.

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: I was like, well, she learned what she learned. That's probably a healthy reaction for having learned what she learned this week. I think the audience was a little surprised.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: Was there a white person in her life that you felt like, uh-oh, if she thinks that about all white people, then she's going to hate this one person who's actually, you know, a nice person?

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: Oh, no, absolutely not. I'm not concerned about the white man in America. I think he's doing very well. And I had no concern, or do I now have any concern for anyone's feelings or whatever else being hurt by a five-year-old. Maybe it could start a conversation with them. They can think about some of the things that they enjoy that no one else enjoy in this country. So no.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: I really like Cliff. Cliff is not an easy person, but then why should he be easy? Cliff is the type of person who keeps the rest of us a little more honest. I want more Cliff in my life.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: Kadijah told me that even with her candid, unfiltered upbringing, she could tell early on the difference between white oppression and the white people in her life. But to be able to do that, she had to learn about it and get angry. I get that.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: When I first began to really understand the violence of racism, I was angry. It makes sense to be angry. The anger helps you push back against the injustice. Anger is not the goal. It's the fuel.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: Even so, sometimes I feel like I have too much anger. There are black people in America dying from racism. Bad treatment in a fancy coffee shop is the softest and easiest part of racism.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: There were times during this whole thing I felt like I should just drop it. Cliff and I talked about that, too.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: Being told to leave a cafe on College Avenue, that's not a big deal on a basic level. But I knew that you can't just keep letting your boundary get pushed.

segments.speaker: Cliff Means
segments.text: I don't let anything go. I don't let anything go. Don't shake my hand like you're black or something. You shake my hand like a white man. You shake my hand like you shake-- don't relate to me.

segments.speaker: W. Kamau Bell
segments.text: Don't let anything go is the message of the day. That's what I feel, but I never put it in those words. Those are the words I was looking for. Don't let anything go.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Racism is real and happening right now, every day. That means that every day I have an opportunity to teach my daughters about racism. So this is to you, Sami and Juno. I promise you, from now on, I'm not going to let it go. The stakes are too high.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: W. Kamau Bell is a comedian in Berkeley. You can hear him on his podcast, "Denzel Washington is the Greatest Actor of All Time Period," or find a list of his upcoming shows on his website, wkamaubell.com. That's W-K-A-M-A-U Bell dot com.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Coming up, a group of grownups who are not fumbling at all. They have a plan, and it includes costumes, volcanoes, and a talking stick. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Chana Joffe-Walt, sitting in for Ira Glass. Today's show, "The Birds and the Bees." We are listening in as grownups try to convey their most important deeply-held beliefs to small humans who cannot yet zip up their own jackets.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: We started at the beginning, where do babies come from? In this last part of the show, we're going to talk about the end. Act Three, "About That Farm Upstate." Jonathan Goldstein has this last story.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And a quick warning, like I said at the beginning of the show, these are stories about grownups talking with children about difficult subject matter. So if you have kids with you, keep that in mind. OK, here's Jonathan.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: There's a house in Salt Lake City where kids come to have death explained to them, not just that people die but how they die. It's called The Sharing Place. And the first person they meet there is Jill Macfarlane. This is how she explains a heart attack.

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: Your heart stopped working, and it couldn't move your blood through your body.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: She has a quiver full of kid-sized explanations for all the ways that life can end, like kidney failure.

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: Your kidneys are washing machines for your blood. And when they stop working and your blood's dirty, then it poisons your body, and you die.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Overdoses.

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: Overdose is when you have a sickness in your brain called addiction. An addiction makes you take medicine that's not good for you, and you take way too much of it. But not all medicine's bad either.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Have you dealt with murder?

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: Mm-hm. It's when somebody chooses to make your body stop working. It's a choice. We also do choice and not choice. Like, murder is a choice. Cancer is not a choice.

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: We also do contagious or not contagious. Like, you're not going to get my depression. And you're not going to get my cancer.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: The Sharing Place is a grief support center for kids who have lost a family member. It's one of hundreds of centers like it around the country. Kids sit in support groups led by grownups, but the point is to allow children to talk to other children about their grief.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: They're encouraged to speak in concrete language about death because, the thinking goes, that's how to process death's finality. So people don't pass away. You don't lose them. They die.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: We invest so much effort trying to shield kids from the scary things in life. We place advisories before TV shows that warn against inappropriate language and subject matter. And what could be less appropriate than death?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: So for all we let on-- bunnies lay eggs. Your mother means well. And life pretty much goes on forever. To do otherwise feels like you're breaking a basic pact that grownups have with one another.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Who did you have die?

segments.speaker: Child 1
segments.text: My dad, two guinea pigs, a dog, two cats, and my dad. And that's all.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: The kids here are more comfortable talking about death than most adults are, like Hailey, who lost a sister and brother to mitochondrial disease. She and her other brother have the disease, too, but not as bad. They've had to deal with something that most other people haven't had too, let alone other kids. So it's hard to talk about with the kids at school.

segments.speaker: Hailey
segments.text: Sometimes they don't even know what we're talking about, because we know all this stuff, like all these words that none of the other kids heard about, like neurological or something like that. And they're like, what does that mean? Or like a feeding tube, what does that mean?

segments.speaker: Child 2
segments.text: It's like really hard to explain.

segments.speaker: Hailey
segments.text: It's not hard to explain, but it's hard to tell them, and they still don't understand where it goes or what it does to help you.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: But this is a place where kids do understand. There are more than a dozen separate the groups at The Sharing Place, broken down by age. The groups meet twice a month for about an hour and a half in a refurbished house, made to feel homey and safe so it's like visiting your grandma's.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: There are rooms where kids meet and talk and rooms where their parents do the same. But most of the rooms are dedicated to play. There's a costume room where kids can dress up like police, ballerinas, cowboys.

segments.speaker: Child 3
segments.text: I'm Spider-Man. So you can do whatever I tell you to do.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And beside it is a room called the soft room, which is full of props and toys, including an old telephone. One little girl who watched her mother have a heart attack spent an entire play session pretending to call for help.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: "Hi, 9-1-1," she'd say. "My grandma's dying. Hurry. Come quick." Then she'd hang up and dial again. "Hi, 9-1-1, my dad's dying. Hurry. Come quick."

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: One of the most popular rooms is a padded room called the volcano room.

segments.speaker: Child 4
segments.text: I'm going to go play in the volcano room.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: It's full of cushions and large rubber yoga balls. It's even got an adult-sized dummy to wrestle and punch. The kids can scream, yell, pound the walls, and throw things around. They love it.

segments.speaker: Child 4
segments.text: Whoo. Bling. Boom. Bam. No ball can attack me. Whoo! Boing.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: It's a release. Eve is nine years old, and her father died about two years ago. She knows that feeling of keeping it all bottled up inside. She says she can go days at school like that.

segments.speaker: Eve
segments.text: It kind of feels really overwhelming. And it's like you don't know what to do. And on the inside, it's like hurting somehow in a feeling way. It like hurts somehow.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Where would you say it hurts?

segments.speaker: Eve
segments.text: Usually, with me, it would hurt in the throat and kind of in my stomach. It's like something that needs to come out, but just I really need to learn how to do that.

segments.speaker: Nancy Reiser
segments.text: I think there are people in this world who can grow up and don't really know how to talk frankly about lots of things.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Nancy Reiser is one of the co-founders of The Sharing Place. And this is what she says when children ask her how people die.

segments.speaker: Nancy Reiser
segments.text: I say, well, close your eyes and listen. [HEAVY BREATHING]

segments.speaker: Nancy Reiser
segments.text: And there isn't the next breath. Does it hurt? I don't think so. I don't think so. Their face doesn't look like it hurt.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Nancy's a therapist who works with young children. For a long time, the very concept that children do, in fact, grieve was hotly disputed. Freud said that it was difficult for children to even conceive of such loss. And as a culture, Nancy says, that's pretty much the idea that we operate under.

segments.speaker: Nancy Reiser
segments.text: Oh, look, she's playing. She's OK. She didn't really understand what happened. Well, she's playing. But then half an hour later, she's in the house, holding her teddy bear and sucking her thumb and crying.

segments.speaker: Nancy Reiser
segments.text: So we need to let people know that children grieve, and help them when they grieve so it's not stuck inside and comes out when they try to have a relationship later. When they start to get intimate, they cannot bear it, and they go off. And they don't know why.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Nancy says children just grieve differently than adults, especially little children. They grieve in fits and starts. They can't focus on it for very long. And grief is more physical for them.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: They'll act out their anger, maybe kick a door, which is the reason for the volcano room at The Sharing Place. They might also regress, suddenly using baby talk or sucking their thumbs. And if they're potty trained, they might become untrained.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: They're also magical thinkers. I heard stories of kids who were afraid to go to sleep because grandma went to sleep and didn't wake up. One little boy wandered away from his mom at the emergency room saying, I'm looking for Dad. We left him here last time. Another boy said he just wanted to die for a few days so he can go to heaven and teach his little sister how to ride a tricycle.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Children also re-grieve. That is, with every new stage of development, they experience their grief anew. And with every milestone-- when their braces come off, when they get their driver's license, when they graduate-- they'll inevitably think, I wish my mom was here.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And given all of this, the thought behind The Sharing Place and other centers like it is that kids can help one another in a way that adults perhaps can't help them. That's why they're brought together in these groups. In short, kids speak the same language.

segments.speaker: Gavin
segments.text: Is that thing turned on?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: It is turned on. What do you think about that?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Before their session at The Sharing Place, I sit down with Gavin, who's six, and his brother, Aidan, who's eight. They're both dressed in matching long-sleeved polo shirts. Gavin sits on his mother Nichole's lap. Aidan sits beside them.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Oh, do you want to introduce yourself?

segments.speaker: Aidan
segments.text: Hi. I'm Aidan. My dad died by--

segments.speaker: Nichole
segments.text: Suicide.

segments.speaker: Aidan
segments.text: Suicide.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: His little brother, Gavin, points his finger to his head and pulls the pretend trigger. He snaps is head back.

segments.speaker: Nichole
segments.text: Yep, that's what happened.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: What did you just do there?

segments.speaker: Gavin
segments.text: He shot his head. And then, we didn't know he was dead, right Mama?

segments.speaker: Nichole
segments.text: We didn't.

segments.speaker: Gavin
segments.text: And then we said, "Wake up, Dad."

segments.speaker: Nichole
segments.text: No, you didn't see him. Mommy found him. And he was already dead.

segments.speaker: Gavin
segments.text: Did you turn him over?

segments.speaker: Nichole
segments.text: I didn't touch him.

segments.speaker: Gavin
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Aidan
segments.text: Because she knew he was dead, because she saw blood and things.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: On his head?

segments.speaker: Aidan
segments.text: Yeah. And he was a terrific guy-- so nice, so generous. He would always help anyone. He was a terrific guy.

segments.speaker: Nichole
segments.text: What did you learn here that helped you the most?

segments.speaker: Aidan
segments.text: To understand how he died.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Sometimes that task, telling the kids that their parent committed suicide, falls to Jill Macfarlane, because the surviving parent or guardian might be so inside their own grief that they can't bring themselves to do it. Jill explains suicide as simply as she does other kinds of death.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: There's a sickness in your brain called depression, she says. And it can make you decide to make your own body stop working. She says it's required that the kids know how their brother or sister or mother died before starting the group.

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: Well, I had one family say he died because he was sick. One family said that he died in a car accident. One family said that he accidentally shot himself. He didn't mean to.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: It was Jill who helped their mom break the news to Aidan and Gavin that their dad shot himself. She says that conversation was especially hard.

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: The boys immediately said, you don't know my dad. Why would you say that? You don't know us.

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: And I said, I know. I don't know you. But your mom's here today because she needed my help in telling you this, because this is a really hard and scary thing that happened. And your mom told me that that's what happened.

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: And Aidan just was like, you're crazy, lady. There's no way that we're going to talk about this. This is not what happened. It was horrible and was awful. And I cried that whole night.

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: It was just awful. I just felt so horrible. And my husband was like, you can't do this. You have to go to the director and tell her that you can't do this again.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Suicide is always one of the highest, if not the highest cause of death for Sharing Place families at any given time. There's actually a special group devoted specifically to suicide.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And a lot of the stories you hear in that group are so horrible that you can't help but wonder, why tell the kids what happened at all? Why not just say they died and leave it at that?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: According to Jill and her colleagues, we need to tell children so they won't find out later in life and wonder, what else did they lie to me about? They also don't want to have to cloak it in a way that suggests it's unspeakable and shameful. They get enough of that idea at school.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: This is Eve again, whose father also shot himself.

segments.speaker: Eve
segments.text: Well, some people at school, they say this makes me feel really sad, too. They say that when somebody kills themselves, that means they go to the wrong place. I don't believe that, but it just makes me feel really sad when they say that. Like instead of going to a happy place, they would go to a sad.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: But even if you don't believe it, and you know it's nonsense, it still kind of hurts that someone would say that?

segments.speaker: Eve
segments.text: Yeah, it does, because it's like somebody judging my papa, which it's not a bad thing. A lot of people do that. But you know, just kind of feels a little weird. Like on the inside, it makes me feel like I'm going to scream and do something like that.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: What are the things that you wish that people would say?

segments.speaker: Eve
segments.text: Probably it's OK that that has happened. And we can help you with feeling better and understanding you. That's probably something I'd want somebody to say.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Once a child knows how their loved one died, they're encouraged to say it out loud. There's a kind of sorcery to it, naming the dragon so you can defeat it.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: I sat in on the suicide group, which is different than the other groups in that kids tend to come to meetings for a longer period of time, partly because they didn't get to say goodbye. The kids sit a circle at the beginning of the meeting and hand around a talking stick. One by one, they say their name, who died, and how they died.

segments.speaker: Elias
segments.text: My name is Elias, and the person who died was my dad. And he died by shooting his self with a gun. And he wanted to die.

segments.speaker: Lindsey
segments.text: Hello, my name is Lindsey. My dad died. He died by suicide. And I regret not seeing him, because I hadn't seen him for a couple of months before his death.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: There's also a different question they respond to each time they meet. What do you miss most about the person? Is there anything you don't miss? Tonight's question is, what do you regret?

segments.speaker: Ethan
segments.text: My name is Ethan, and the person who died is my dad. He died by shooting his self in the head. And I don't know if I have any regrets. I just can't remember.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: It can take a long time for them to get to this point, where they can say the word suicide. The Sharing Place never corrects any of the kids or forces them to say anything they don't want to. But they notice when a child is finally able to say it.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: The night I was there, Aidan, the nine-year-old I talked to who had a hard time saying the word suicide, was finally able to say it in group.

segments.speaker: Volunteer 1
segments.text: So how about Aidan?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: The volunteers sat around and talked about it afterwards.

segments.speaker: Volunteer 1
segments.text: It was hard for him, I could tell. He wasn't about to say it, but he said it. And I was proud of him. But it took him probably at least a minute to actually get those words out.

segments.speaker: Volunteer 2
segments.text: And he had to ask his mom if it was OK to say.

segments.speaker: Volunteer 3
segments.text: So she wasn't coaching him?

segments.speaker: Volunteer 1
segments.text: Nope.

segments.speaker: Volunteer 2
segments.text: No. He was good.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: On the other hand, Aidan's brother, Gavin, the six-year-old, talks about his dad's suicide incessantly. He also draws guns during playtime and even sculpts them out of Play-Doh. This is Jill Macfarlane again.

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: He tells everybody at school, "My dad shot his brains." And it freaks everybody out. And so then he gets in trouble at school, which then he was like, well, I guess I can't ever talk about my dad.

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: But this is how kindergartners talk and process things. It's just easy for them to talk about. But it scares other people.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Is it OK for other kids in their class to hear that kind of thing?

segments.speaker: Jill Macfarlane
segments.text: Well, yeah. I mean, is there a right answer to that? I don't know.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: I don't know either. If I were a parent, I'm not sure I'd want my kid hearing that kind of thing at school. And while Jill doesn't have an answer, she does think kids being allowed to express themselves is much healthier than sending them a message that it's wrong to say this kind of stuff out loud. And that's got to be a step in the right direction.

segments.speaker: Sara Mohammed
segments.text: I have very, very, very fond memories of this place. I actually tried to come through the side door, because that was the door that I always came in through. Then I was like, I can use the adult entrance, finally.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Sara Mohammed hasn't been to The Sharing Place for a full six years. She's 21 now. But when she was 11, her older brother hanged himself.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Even though he was supposed to be babysitting her, her parents had told her to keep an eye out on him because of his past suicide attempts. Obviously what happened wasn't her fault, but she blamed herself, which is something I heard other kids here talk about too.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: It's easy for an adult to say, don't be silly. It's not your fault. But it's a whole other thing to talk with a kid at The Sharing Place who says, I know exactly what you're talking about.

segments.speaker: Sara Mohammed
segments.text: It was kind of nice seeing the older kids whose loved ones had been gone for a few years, how they were able to go to school normally and just live their normal lives, because I just didn't want to go to school. I didn't want to be with kids who just didn't know. It was too hard.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: I asked Sara if there was a turning point, a moment when she began to feel like maybe she was doing a little better. She said, yes. She was in the courtyard with a bunch of other kids.

segments.speaker: Sara Mohammed
segments.text: We were just out there painting rocks or something for a fundraiser. And we were just talking, just talking like normal. And I realized that I hadn't had a conversation like that in about a year, just where I felt 100% free, and just laughing and not feeling guilty about laughing, and just happy. And yeah, that was really the first time in a good nine months after my brother had passed that I felt OK.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: It's the kids themselves who decide when they're ready to stop coming to The Sharing Place. But on average, they stay about two years. When they're ready to leave, they have to announce their intention two times in group before their final goodbye.

segments.speaker: Volunteer 4
segments.text: Any of you that would like to say something to him, which I'm sure several of you will?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: The goodbye is ceremonial. And on the last night I was there, at the end of the meeting, they said goodbye to a kid name Robby. He sat in the circle with the other kids and volunteers. And anybody who wanted to could pick up the talking stick and say a few words. His friend, Jessica, was the last kid to do so.

segments.speaker: Jessica
segments.text: I'll definitely miss you, because you're like one of my best friends in this group. And I'll miss seeing you. And our major fight that we had in the volcano room, it was not my fault.

segments.speaker: Robby
segments.text: You asked for it.

segments.speaker: Jessica
segments.text: No I didn't.

segments.speaker: Robby
segments.text: Yes, you did.

segments.speaker: Jessica
segments.text: No. It was just really fun, and I'm going to miss seeing you and miss hanging out with you.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: At Robby's last meeting, there was a kid who'd just shown up. It was his first meeting. He had long bangs hanging over his eyes and, except for his name, didn't say anything the whole time.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Whenever a new person joins, the veteran kids have a chance to gauge their own progress, to remember what they were like when they first showed up, and think about how bad it used to be, and how now it isn't as bad. And ultimately, like Robby, they'll make way for someone on the long waiting list, a list on which new names are added all the time. They'll say, "I think it's time to go." And then they'll say it again.
